title: Malaysia suspends recruitment of workers from Nepal — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Malaysia suspends recruitment of workers from Nepal — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Malaysia has suspended the recruitment of unskilled workers from Nepal due to a dispute over the procedure for selecting recruitment agencies. As Kathmandu Post reports, on October 1, Malaysia’s Ministry of Human Resources halted biomedical examinations for job candidates, effectively stopping the issuance of new employment visas.

Dispute over agencies

Visa processing under Malaysia’s foreign worker management system requires medical reports from 36 accredited centres in Nepal. The system operator, Bestinet, said registration for examinations would resume after 25 main recruitment agencies selected by Kuala Lumpur are activated. Each of them is to work together with ten auxiliary agencies.

Nepal’s Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment objected to the unilateral selection of 25 agencies and refused to grant them legal authorization for exclusive operations. Minister Ramji Yadav proposed holding a Joint Working Group meeting on November 18–19 or December 2–3 to discuss the worker recruitment mechanism and the renewal of the bilateral memorandum.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

However, Malaysia’s Minister of Human Resources, Ramanan Ramakrishnan, said in a letter conveyed through diplomatic channels on October 6 that the country’s government would not change the current model. Malaysia will retain the selection of 25 main agencies and ten auxiliary agencies for each of them.

Proceedings in Nepal

At the same time, Nepal’s Department of Foreign Employment launched legal action against the owners of the 25 selected agencies. The agency said it had obtained warrants from the Foreign Employment Tribunal and ordered individuals for whom warrants had been issued and who had not appeared before the authorities to report to the department or police within 35 days. Failure to comply may result in further procedures, including the freezing of bank accounts and restrictions on exit permits.

In the previous fiscal year, Malaysia accepted 132,000 Nepali workers. According to Nepal’s central bank, Malaysia accounts for nearly 20% of remittances to the country, while about 400,000 Nepali citizens work there, mainly in the manufacturing sector.

title: Two-day weekends in Nepal boost resort bookings to 40–50% — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Two-day weekends in Nepal boost resort bookings to 40–50% — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, two-day weekends introduced by the government in April have contributed to the growth of domestic tourism. Hotels and resorts near Kathmandu report more active weekend bookings, Kathmandu Post writes.

Weekend trips

Binayak Shah, president of the Hotel Association Nepal, said that Nepalis' travel habits have changed. According to him, popular destinations for short trips include Pokhara, Dhulikhel and Nagarkot near the Kathmandu Valley. Couples aged 25 to 45, families with schoolchildren and groups of friends travelling by private cars are taking trips more often.

Amita Shrestha, sales and marketing manager at Mystic Mountain Resort in Nagarkot, said it has become easier for guests to plan holidays. Previously, they had to leave after a shortened working day on Friday, but now they can arrive on Saturday and return on Sunday. According to her, weekend bookings have increased to 40–50%.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Demand beyond the Kathmandu Valley

Ram Sundar Bake, president of the Bagmati chapter of the Hotel Association Nepal, noted that hotels and resorts are now sometimes fully booked on Fridays and Saturdays. Tourists are also travelling more often farther from the Kathmandu Valley — to the Malkot area in Sindhuli, Bandipur, Gorkha and Nuwakot. In his view, this stimulates rural tourism and the promotion of tourist destinations.

Arun Shrestha, founder of Prakriti Resort and Organic Farm, reported that the number of domestic tourists and hiking enthusiasts at the establishment in Haibung, Sindhupalchok district, has increased by up to 50%. At the same time, in Dhulikhel, the effect of the new policy is being constrained by delays in the Bhaktapur–Suryabinayak–Dhulikhel road project, as well as the consequences of floods and landslides.

The Hotel Association Nepal believes that extended weekends are shaping a culture of domestic travel, popularising lesser-known destinations and supporting the local economy — from farmers and transport operators to hotels.

title: Drone kills Nepali worker in Saudi Arabia — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Drone kills Nepali worker in Saudi Arabia — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Saudi Arabia, 45-year-old Nepali labor migrant Bharat Mahato was killed in a drone attack on October 21. He worked as a cleaner at a Saudi Aramco project site in the kingdom's Eastern Province. As Kathmandu Post reports, a drone launched by Yemen's Houthis struck the site, where workers from Pakistan and India were also killed.

The deceased man's wife, 41-year-old Indrika Devi Mahato, said that she initially received a call from a supervisor at the site, who told her that her husband had been injured and hospitalized. Later, the family was informed of Mahato's death. On the eve of the attack, he made his final video call to his wife and asked her to take care of the children.

Family asks for the body to be returned

Bharat Mahato had worked abroad for 14 years and was the main breadwinner for his family in the village of Dhekaha in Nepal's Mahottari district. He sent home about 20,000 rupees every month, including to repay a bank loan for the construction of a four-room concrete house.

Indrika Mahato took out a bank loan of 1.1 million rupees to build the house. She must now raise four children on her own and repay the debt. The family submitted an application to the district administration in Jaleshwar, asking the Nepalese authorities to help repatriate the body.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

According to Indradev Yadav, head of the district administration, the appeal was forwarded to the Ministry of Home Affairs, which is to send it to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to begin the procedure for returning the body. The consular department has already transferred the case to Nepal's embassy in Riyadh, which has received Mahato's death certificate.

Payments unavailable to the family

The family will be unable to receive standard financial assistance from Nepal's Foreign Employment Board and a term life insurance payment. The reason is that Mahato's work permit expired a year before his death. These programs usually provide payments of about 1 million and 1.5 million rupees, respectively.

Nepal's embassy in Riyadh urged the country's citizens in Saudi Arabia not to go outside during danger warnings, to follow official announcements by the Saudi authorities, and not to spread unverified information. According to the publication's estimate, about 400,000 Nepalese citizens work in Saudi Arabia.

title: Bracing For Cyclone - The Rising Nepal
description: Bracing For Cyclone  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Almost two weeks have gone by since the monsoon withdrew from Nepal but the country is now staring at another unusual climatic event. The cyclone in the Bay of Bengal is going to have an impact on the weather pattern in Nepal from Wednesday evening. Even though the cyclone may weaken when moving inland, it can have a negative effect on the region due to the possibility of rain, landslides, floods, and other weather-related problems. Since rainfall is expected in several provinces starting from Thursday, the government and local authorities must take the required actions right now. As a mountainous country, it means that any precipitation can become a great danger to some areas in the country due to the nature of the area, poor urbanisation and rivers filled with water due to rainfall. It is especially true for the regions in the hills, Chure and the Tarai, since flash floods, landslides and waterlogging are likely to occur there. Additionally, in the high Himalayas, there is a risk of heavy snowfall, snowstorms, and avalanches.

This forecast gives a warning for carrying out preparations. There are warnings that water levels in big river basins may start rising from Thursday, with certain rivers reaching the levels of warning and vigilance by Friday and Saturday. Such warnings must be immediately followed by some actions taken, not just announced. The government should be able to spot potential settlements, check the drainage system, clear any blockages in waterways and make sure evacuation routes and temporary shelters are set up. Security, medical personnel and other emergency responders should stand ready in risky places. But in some cases, it seems like the response to disaster is always reactive – only when a threat is present or some damage occurs.

There are warnings being given, advisories being sent out, and emergency meetings held, but all these activities depend on whether such measures will help vulnerable settlements. A forecast does not mean anything if the villagers beside the swollen river do not know when to leave or where to go to hide from the rain. This means that communication between meteorological authorities and district and local governments is paramount. Warnings should be disseminated in simple, understandable terms via many mediums like local radios, mobile phones and community alerts and networks. Special consideration must be paid to remote locations where there might be a lack of proper communication and rough terrain that may hinder help from reaching. It is equally important to verify whether rescue equipment, medicines, food and potable water are available. Farming communities are facing another immediate problem. Paddy harvest time has already arrived, and rainfall at this stage can lead to crop destruction and delayed harvests.

Authorities should assist farmers in assessing more vulnerable farming communities and providing them with timely weather updates. This step is necessary from the point of view of agriculture and also for the livelihood and food security of farming families. The people of the region need to take the warnings very seriously. They should refrain from crossing flooded rivers, moving around landslide-prone roads and entering high mountains of the Himalayas during the storm. Vulnerable families should stock up on necessities and prepare to move to safer ground. Firstly, the most important thing about this weather pattern is that it should be seen as a litmus test for Nepal’s preparedness for disasters. Extreme weather conditions can sometimes be inevitable, but the damage they cause can be controlled with appropriate warnings, effective actions, and responsible behaviour from people.

title: Thousands of EVs stranded at Korola - The Rising Nepal
description: Thousands of EVs stranded at Korola  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By our correspondent,Muktinath (Mustang), Oct. 28: Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) booked during the festive season have remained stranded for a long time at the Korala border point, customs office and various locations along the road.

A total of 3,122 EVs that entered Nepal through the Liji–Nechung (Korala) border point via Tibet, China, are stranded in Mustang, while some others are stranded along the Pokhara–Beni–Jomsom road section. After floods, landslides, and river erosion damaged the Beni–Jomsom–Korala road, the Traffic Police have started using bulldozers to remove vehicles stuck in muddy sections or involved in accidents.

According to Santosh Basyal, information officer at the District Police Office, Mustang, 2,828 EVs are stranded in the no-man’s-land area at the Korala border point, 120 in the customs yard, 75 at the charging station in Charang, 45 on private land in Chhoser, 23 in Ghansa due to the absence of drivers, and 19 at the Jomsom bus park.

Inspector Basyal said that the authorities had been urging owners to remove vehicles that had remained on the road for a long time. “We understand that there is a problem with charging,” he said.

More than 30 EVs are also stranded on the road at various locations along the Korala–Jomsom section.

Despite clear weather and the resumption of road traffic, the concerned authorities have not provided any information about the condition of the vehicles that have remained stranded for an extended period.

The Mustang Customs Office said that a charging station was available in Charang, Ward No. 1 of Lo-Ghyakar Damodarkunda Rural Municipality in Upper Mustang, but additional charging stations are needed at other locations. As they have not yet been installed, the EVs have had to remain stranded for a long time even after completing customs clearance.

EVs also account for a significant share of the customs office’s revenue.

The Korala border point is connected to Kushma Municipality-1, Pang in Parbat district, via Beni in Myagdi, covering a distance of 202 km. Situated at an altitude of 4,650 metres above sea level, the Korala border point is about 14 kilometres uphill from the customs office.

After completing customs clearance, the vehicles are transported to Pokhara along the 186-km Kaligandaki Corridor, through the Beni–Jomsom–Korala road section. However, the muddy road has also been causing damage to EVs during transportation, said Ghar Chung Gurung, vice-chairperson of the Korala Border Point Container Management Committee.

Preparations have been made to ensure that all EVs cleared through customs at Korala are transported out of the district before Tihar. Likewise, customs representatives of EV sellers in Nepal have also said that arrangements are being made to move the stranded vehicles. According to Tejaswi Sharma, chief of the Kaligandaki Road Project, there have been no major problems with the daily movement of small vehicles along the road section.

At present, vehicles carrying customs-cleared goods intended for the festive season, as well as apples and other goods from Mustang, are leaving the district daily. The District Police Office, Mustang, said that 27 containers were still stranded at various locations in the district as of Monday evening.

title: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News - Khabarhub
description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Nepal’s economic outlook presents a mixed picture, with modest stock market gains and continued investment activity contrasted by significant disaster-related losses and growing pressure on public resources. NEPSE edged up 0.94 points to 2,630.76, while turnover increased to Rs 5.79 billion. However, declining share prices across several sectors suggest that market confidence remains uneven. Gold prices also rose, reflecting continued movement in domestic commodity markets.

The August 26 floods in the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river basins remain a major economic concern. Private property and business losses reached Rs 79.17 billion, while insurers have disbursed only Rs 821.3 million against registered claims initially estimated at Rs 20.904 billion. The government’s relief funds hold Rs 18.136 billion, but effective recovery will depend on transparent distribution, timely insurance settlements and coordinated reconstruction efforts.

Policy measures offer some support for economic stability. Nepal Rastra Bank’s borrower advisory emphasizes responsible lending, while Gavi’s Rs 8.59 billion assistance strengthens immunization financing. Tourism arrivals in the Annapurna Conservation Area and through Kakarbhitta indicate continued travel demand. Meanwhile, declining profits at NIFRA and proposed civil service retirement provisions highlight institutional and financial challenges.

Overall, Nepal needs stronger disaster resilience, efficient public spending, responsible credit management and sustained investment to support recovery and long-term economic stability.

NEPSE edges up 0.94 points as turnover reaches Rs 5.79 billion

The Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index gained 0.94 points to close at 2,630.76 on Tuesday, the second trading day following the Dashain holiday. Share prices of 135 companies rose, while 136 declined and eight remained unchanged. Daily turnover climbed to Rs 5.79 billion from Rs 4 billion on Monday. Ghalemdi Hydropower, People’s Hydropower, Sanima Middle Tamor Hydropower, Liberty Energy, Green Ventures, Himalayan Distillery and Api Power recorded the highest trading volumes. The hydropower sub-index posted the strongest gain, rising 1.65 percent, while most other sectoral indices ended lower. Beni Hydropower led individual gainers with a 15 percent increase, followed by Upper Mailung Khola Hydropower, which rose 12.09 percent. Life insurance declined 0.59 percent, while hotels and tourism fell 0.51 percent. Unilever Nepal was among the biggest losers, with its share price dropping 4.91 percent.

Gold price rises to Rs 282,300 per tola, silver falls to Rs 3,970

Gold prices increased in Nepal’s domestic market on Tuesday, while silver prices declined, according to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association. The price of hallmark gold rose by Rs 800 per tola, reaching Rs 282,300. The metal had traded at Rs 281,500 per tola on Monday. In contrast, silver fell by Rs 25 per tola to Rs 3,970, down from Rs 3,995 on the previous day.

Bhote Koshi floods cause Rs 79.17 billion in private property losses: NPC

Private property and business losses caused by the August 26 floods in the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river basins have reached Rs 79.17 billion, according to a finalized assessment by the National Planning Commission (NPC). The report estimates household losses at Rs 69.57 billion and damage to commercial enterprises at Rs 9.60 billion. Residential land covering 54.65 hectares sustained losses valued at Rs 13.26 billion, while housing construction losses amounted to Rs 11.95 billion. Damage to 507.97 hectares of privately owned land was estimated at Rs 35.44 billion. Agricultural losses included crop damage worth Rs 232.1 million affecting 2,951 farming families. Stored food grains worth Rs 10.41 billion were lost, while livestock and fisheries suffered damage estimated at Rs 21.42 billion. Vehicle losses amounted to Rs 1.24 billion, and losses involving cultural artefacts and jewellery reached Rs 5 billion. The assessment also found that 3,187 households lost durable goods worth Rs 1.45 billion, while 2,769 families lost non-durable household items valued at Rs 663.5 million. The floods affected 6,817 families and 32,872 people across 15 local units in Dhading, Gorkha, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts. A total of 499 business establishments were also affected, while 2,989 residential structures were completely destroyed.

NRB urges borrowers to assess financial capacity and credit risks

Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) has issued a public financial literacy advisory urging borrowers to assess their repayment capacity, income, collateral requirements and loan terms before taking out loans from financial institutions. Highlighting the five Cs of credit assessment used by banks—cash flow, capital, character and credit history, collateral, and loan conditions—the central bank outlined five key stages of borrowing: loan application, borrower assessment, credit approval, loan disbursement and monitoring of loan utilization. It also advised borrowers to use loans for productive purposes and make repayments on time.

Parliamentary committee seeks detailed relief reports from 49 flood-hit wards

The National Assembly’s Special Parliamentary Committee on Disaster Studies and Monitoring in the Bhote Koshi and Kali Gandaki river basins has directed government agencies to submit detailed reports on flood damage and relief distribution across 49 affected wards. Committee Chair Krishna Prasad Paudel said during Tuesday’s meeting that field inspections could not proceed effectively without verified district- and ward-level data endorsed by local ward chairs. The reports are expected to cover financial assistance, food distribution, humanitarian losses, missing persons, displaced people, agricultural damage and disruptions to communication networks. The committee has scheduled consultations with relevant ministers through November 2 to assess coordination among government agencies, damage estimates, reconstruction funding, management of the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, international humanitarian assistance and the deployment of security personnel. Following the consultations, the committee plans to conduct field inspections in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading from November 3 to 21.

Insurers pay Rs 821.3 million in claims for Bhote Koshi and Trishuli flood damage

General insurance companies have disbursed Rs 821.3 million in advance payments and interim settlements for damage to infrastructure, vehicles and commercial property caused by the August 26 floods in the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river basins. According to the Nepal Insurance Authority, 2,491 claims have been registered, with estimated losses initially assessed at Rs 20.904 billion. Himalayan Everest Insurance recorded 209 claims worth Rs 6.615 billion, the highest claim value among the reported insurers, and has paid Rs 232.3 million. Among individual companies, Sagarmatha Lumbini Insurance made the largest total payout, disbursing Rs 266.3 million against claims worth Rs 1.759 billion. Shikhar Insurance paid Rs 214.7 million against claims totaling Rs 2.639 billion. By insurance category, property insurance accounted for claims worth Rs 9.563 billion from 576 policyholders, with Rs 162.8 million disbursed. Engineering insurance recorded claims of Rs 4.401 billion from 174 claimants, with Rs 174 million paid. Motor insurance accounted for 1,067 claims worth Rs 2.848 billion, with Rs 236.6 million disbursed. Marine transit insurance recorded claims totaling Rs 2.335 billion, of which Rs 238.9 million has been settled. The Nepal Insurance Authority has also issued an eight-point directive requiring insurers to ease documentation requirements for life insurance death claims, declarations of missing persons and replacement of lost policy certificates. The directive also provides for a six-month interest-free grace period for premium payments and loan instalments to ease the financial burden on flood-affected policyholders.

Agriculture office urges farmers to manage harvests ahead of forecast rainfall

The Agriculture Development Office has urged farmers to monitor weather forecasts and adjust harvesting schedules ahead of rainfall expected in several parts of the country from October 28 to November 1. The office advised farmers to harvest mature paddy crops immediately or wait until after November 1. Farmers with crops that have yet to ripen were advised to drain excess water from their fields and bundle lodged stalks to prevent grain submersion and reduce potential crop losses from adverse weather.

Department of Foreign Employment gives suspects 35 days to contact authorities

The Department of Foreign Employment has issued a public notice directing individuals facing warrants from the Foreign Employment Tribunal to contact the department or Nepal Police within 35 days to comply with legal proceedings. The notice warns that failure to respond could result in legal consequences, including restrictions on travel authorizations and the freezing of bank transactions. The department said fraudulent job offers, unauthorized fee collection, fake demand letters and irregular employment contracts harm migrant workers and their families. The notice aims to expedite pending cases, strengthen accountability and protect workers’ rights through coordination among relevant agencies.

NEA issues electrical safety warning ahead of forecast cyclonic weather

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has urged the public to exercise caution around electrical infrastructure amid forecasts of rainfall and snowfall associated with an approaching cyclonic system on October 30 and 31. The authority warned that adverse weather could damage power infrastructure and disrupt electricity transmission and distribution. It said emergency maintenance teams had been placed on standby at regional distribution centres to respond to outages and restore services. The public has been advised to stay away from hazardous areas around electrical installations and promptly report any damage to power infrastructure.

Parliamentary committee calls for round-the-clock operations at Birgunj dry port

A parliamentary committee has called for improved operational efficiency at the Birgunj Dry Port and the Birgunj Integrated Check Post following an on-site inspection by House of Representatives Infrastructure Development Committee Chair Ashish Gajurel and lawmaker Arbind Sah. The visit assessed infrastructure, management and operational procedures at facilities operated by the Transit and Warehouse Management Company. During discussions with senior officials, the committee representatives stressed the need to keep gates open around the clock to accommodate the movement of approximately 110 cargo trains each month through the dry port and 800 freight vehicles daily through the integrated check post. They also highlighted the importance of railway infrastructure in facilitating the transportation of imported chemical fertilizers.

Prime Minister’s relief funds hold Rs 18.136 billion in contributions

The combined balance of the Prime Minister’s Natural Disaster Relief Fund and the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund reached Rs 18.136 billion as of 9 am on Tuesday, following contributions and financial assistance in the aftermath of the Rasuwa and Bhote Koshi floods. According to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, accounts held at nine commercial banks contain Rs 13.494 billion. Foreign currency accounts maintained at Himalayan Bank and Laxmi Sunrise Bank hold more than USD 30.5 million. The funds are intended to support disaster relief and related assistance efforts.

Minister Rawal pledges additional staff to speed up land ownership certificates

Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation Pratibha Rawal has pledged to deploy additional administrative staff to accelerate the distribution of land ownership certificates and address longstanding housing concerns affecting landless Dalits, squatters and people living in informal settlements. Following discussions with municipal chief administrative officers and local land committee officials, Rawal said delays in service delivery often stemmed from a lack of institutional commitment rather than regulatory obstacles. She said her direct consultations with stakeholders during regional visits were aimed at ensuring transparent grievance handling and more effective public services.

Gavi provides Nepal with Rs 8.59 billion in vaccine assistance through 2030

Nepal has secured vaccine and financial assistance worth Rs 8.591 billion from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to support its routine immunization programme through 2030 following negotiations led by the Ministry of Health. In a separate development, a dispute over historical assistance allocations covering fiscal years 2016/17 to 2021/22 has been resolved, with a previously contested repayment demand of USD 308,271 waived in full. The assistance is expected to support the continuity of Nepal’s national immunization programme and preventive healthcare services aimed at protecting children and other target populations from infectious diseases.

Kakarbhitta border checkpoint records 1,106 foreign tourist arrivals in three months

A total of 1,106 foreign tourists entered Nepal through the Kakarbhitta border checkpoint over a three-month period, according to immigration office data. Of these, 605 arrived between September 17 and October 17. The visitors represented 53 countries, with Bhutan accounting for 478 arrivals, followed by the United States with 242, Australia with 49, Great Britain with 40 and Bangladesh with 35. The checkpoint recorded an average of 12 arrivals daily, rising to 19 during the peak autumn tourism period. During the same three months, the immigration office issued 992 tourist visas, 75 relationship visas, eight marriage visas, 13 non-resident visas and eight SAARC endorsement visas. A total of 985 foreign nationals departed Nepal through the checkpoint during the period.

464 civil servants resign amid proposed retirement provisions

A total of 464 civil servants, including four secretaries, have resigned since the beginning of the current fiscal year on July 17, 2026, according to the National Civil Service Records Office. The office reported that the resignations included 207 gazetted officers, comprising four secretaries, 33 joint secretaries, 72 undersecretaries and 98 section officers. Another 257 non-gazetted employees resigned, including 137 first- and second-class administrative assistants and 120 personnel in unclassified service categories. Although the employees cited personal and family reasons in their resignation letters, officials said the increase followed proposed provisions in the federal civil service bill tabled in the House of Representatives. The proposed legislation would require civil servants to retire upon completing 30 years of service or reaching the age of 55.

Annapurna Conservation Area welcomes 32,963 foreign tourists in a month

The Annapurna Conservation Area recorded 32,963 foreign tourist visits during a one-month period, including 12,645 visitors from South Asian countries and 20,318 from other nations, according to the Annapurna Conservation Area Project. The total represented an increase of 2,416 visitors compared with the 30,547 recorded during the corresponding period last year. However, the reporting period provided in the source requires verification, as the dates are listed as September 17 to August 17. Covering approximately 7,600 square kilometres across 15 local government units in Kaski, Lamjung, Manang, Myagdi and Mustang, the conservation area attracts trekkers during the autumn season. Popular destinations include the Annapurna Circuit, Thorong La Pass, Tilicho Lake and Upper Mustang.

Kathmandu Valley expects Rs 480 million in flower garland sales during Tihar

The Kathmandu Valley is expected to consume approximately 5.2 million flower garlands during the upcoming Tihar festival, generating an estimated market turnover of Rs 480 million, according to the Floriculture Association Nepal. The association expects domestic production to meet most of the demand. Marigold garlands are projected to account for 4.5 million units, with an estimated wholesale value of Rs 405 million at Rs 90 per garland. Globe amaranth, locally known as makhamali, garlands are expected to generate Rs 27 million from 600,000 units priced at Rs 45 each. The forecast also includes 20,000 chrysanthemum garlands valued at Rs 24 million at Rs 1,200 each, and 60,000 mixed-flower garlands worth Rs 2.4 million at Rs 400 each. Meanwhile, the association will organise its 19th Godavari Flower Competitive Exhibition in Jawalakhel, Lalitpur, from October 29 to November 2. The event will feature 78 commercial stalls showcasing 450 varieties of flowers.

Everest Paper Mills workers receive Rs 63.6 million in unpaid wages and benefits

A total of 174 workers at Everest Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. have received Rs 63.6 million in overdue wages and employment benefits, bringing a longstanding labour dispute closer to resolution following prolonged administrative and legal proceedings. On March 31, 2026, the Labour Court ordered the release of Rs 58.6 million. After the employer failed to comply, the court ordered the freezing of shareholders’ accounts on September 11, 2026. The total settlement included the court-ordered arrears and unpaid wages for two months dating back to mid-August. Payments were made through bank cheques on October 16, settling the outstanding claims.

Standard Chartered Bank Nepal proposes 16 percent cash dividend

Standard Chartered Bank Nepal has proposed a cash dividend of 16 percent of its existing paid-up capital for shareholders. The proposed distribution is subject to approval from Nepal Rastra Bank and endorsement by shareholders at the bank’s upcoming annual general meeting. The date of the meeting has not yet been announced. In the previous fiscal year, the bank distributed a cash dividend of 19 percent to its shareholders.

Govt allocates Rs 35 million to support culturally significant films

The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology has announced Rs 35 million in subsidies for film production during fiscal year 2026/27, aiming to promote original, realistic and public awareness-oriented films highlighting Nepal’s cultural heritage and national identity. Under the Procedure on Providing Promotional Subsidies for Film Production in Areas of Cultural and National Significance, 2026, individuals and organisations can apply within 21 days. The programme covers three categories: scriptwriting, production and post-production. The initiative aims to encourage filmmakers to document local cultures, traditions and social realities while supporting projects from script development through final production.

NIFRA’s first-quarter net profit falls 20 percent to Rs 166.4 million

Nepal Infrastructure Bank Ltd. (NIFRA) reported a 20 percent year-on-year decline in net profit to Rs 166.4 million in the first quarter of the current fiscal year, according to its unaudited financial statements. The bank had earned Rs 208.5 million during the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year. The decline was attributed primarily to a fall in net interest income. However, the reported figures contain an apparent discrepancy: net interest income is stated to have declined from Rs 373 million to Rs 34.42 billion, a figure that requires verification. NIFRA’s annualised earnings per share stood at Rs 3.08, while its net worth per share was reported at Rs 112.38. The source also lists paid-up capital of Rs 216 million and accumulated reserves of Rs 2.673 billion; these figures should be checked against the bank’s published financial statements.

title: Kathmandu Film Festival 2026 - Nepali Times
description: Kathmandu Film Festival 2026  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The first ever Kathmandu Film Festival (KFF) 2026 organised by the Metropolitan City will take place from 30 October to 1 November, putting Nepal’s capital on the world’s cinema map.

The festival will showcase 40 feature films and documentaries from 14 countries, and will be screened at the City Hall and Jai Nepal Cinema.

Ten films have been shortlisted for the International Panorama Program, a curated selection of global, contemporary, and independent cinema that represents powerful stories, unique voices and distinct cultural perspectives.

Still from Dear You

The Nepal Panorama Shorts Program will feature nine films. A special retrospective will celebrate Nepali cinema of the 1970s and 80s, including Kumari, the first Nepali feature film in colour.

KFF will also feature a screening of shorts ‘View People, View Cities' from Yamagata, a UNESCO Creative City of Film in Japan to mark 70 years of bilateral ties between Nepal and Japan.

KFF will feature a conversation with noted Indian actor Shabana Azmi on the theme ‘Film, Festivals and A Life Well Lived’. There will be a masterclass ‘The Importance of Film Aesthetics from the Global South and the International Festival Circuit’ with Marco Mueller of the Shanghai Film Academy, and panel discussions Nepal’s film industry itself.

Still from Enchanted Matter

Each film selected will receive a prize of Rs100,000. The top three films will receive additional cash awards of Rs150,000, Rs100,000 and Rs50,000. Films to be screened include: The King’s Warden (Korea), Dear You (China), Bayaan (India), La Gradiva (France), and even the classic, The Godfather.

Among documentaries to be screened will be Enchanted Matter, the Art of Robert Powell, and other short films.

Kathmandu was designated a UNESCO Film City in 2023. Entry to festival screenings and events is free.

title: Household Obligations - The Rising Nepal
description: Household Obligations  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
We recently celebrated Dashain, one of the most auspicious festivals of Nepal. And we are looking forward to celebrating another important festival, Tihar. Festivals might be a time for Nepalis to relax and let their hair down, but are we inadvertently overlooking the strain it puts on women tending to the households?

Nepal might be looking to step up to modernity, but like the rest of the world, it remains patriarchal to the core. Modern women in Nepal are in quite a bind—working outside the home while also keeping up the household. Young girls grow up watching their mothers, aunts, and sisters toil at home, especially during festivals. Sure, it is fun to collaborate on making lunch and dinner with the whole family once in a while, but doing it solo for the rest of the year can be taxing.

Rare are those households where the male members also participate in the household chores. Unequivocally, females are assigned the task of maintaining the house. And in festivals such as Dashain, this means thorough cleaning and washing. The floors have to be swept, the windows cleaned, and the dishes and clothes washed. Next, there is regular cooking. Slack a little in the cooking department and then you get criticism from the rest of the family. Little ones have to be taken care of. Then some teenage children have to be kept entertained while also being educated. Caught up in endless chores, the women in the family rarely have time for themselves. Instead, parties have to be organised while keeping everything in place.

Simone de Beauvoir in the 1950s argued that women aren’t born but made. Decades later, after the rise of the internet, smartphones, social media, and advances in science, it still holds. Young girls grow up to be women believing their place in the world is in relation to a man. It requires constant renegotiation and sacrifice. Give up your time for others. Prioritise others above self. Make sure there is food on the table every day. Moreover, be responsible for the happiness of the rest of the family. It is no wonder that behind every joyful greeting of festivals such as Dashain and Tihar, there is the silent wailing of women in a collective despair.

The question then is how to make the lives of women easier. And the answer is pretty simple: men have to step up in their roles beyond patriarchal norms. If a young girl grows up seeing her father assist her mother through little but meaningful actions such as getting the groceries, helping prep the meal, or even giving the mother a peaceful time of her own, then the girl will acknowledge the importance of a positive support system.

Life is not easy, but a shared burden is easier to bear. Just as charity begins at home, so does gender equality. Parents can set standards for their children through their equal partnership. Through daily acts of kindness between the parents, the children learn that relationships are about equal care, responsibilities, and love. The world will be a better place when people are first human beings rather than their respective genders. As such, let festivals be a time of celebration for women, not an imposition.

title: Nepal Suspends New Trekking Permits in Restricted Himalayan Areas Amid Snowstorm and Avalanche Risk - www.nationpathindia.com
description: Nepal Suspends New Trekking Permits in Restricted Himalayan Areas Amid Snowstorm and Avalanche Risk  www.nationpathindia.com
publisher.title: www.nationpathindia.com
full_article:
Kathmandu — Nepal has introduced a temporary trekking-permit restriction for high-risk mountain areas as authorities prepare for potentially hazardous weather conditions later this week. The Department of Immigration announced that new permits for restricted trekking areas would not be issued for October 29, 30 and 31. The measure is intended to reduce exposure to dangerous conditions as weather warnings indicate a heightened possibility of heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches in high-altitude regions.

Editorial Insight Key Highlights Important points readers should notice. Issue/Event: Temporary suspension of new trekking permits for restricted high-altitude areas. Location: High-hill and Himalayan regions of Nepal. Authority/Organisation: Department of Immigration and National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Action Taken: New permits suspended for October 29–31, with trekkers urged to avoid hazardous journeys and remain in safe locations. - Impact: The measure may affect trekking plans and travel arrangements while mountain weather risks remain elevated.

The warning is linked to Cyclone Arnab, which is affecting weather forecasts across parts of South Asia. Although the cyclone is expected to make landfall along India’s Andhra Pradesh coast, its wider weather effects could combine with other atmospheric conditions to bring rain and snowfall to Nepal. Authorities have urged tourists, trekking agencies, guides and other stakeholders to follow the advisory. Trekkers who have already entered restricted mountain areas have been advised to suspend their journeys and remain in safe locations until conditions improve. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has separately warned of potential weather-related disruptions to transport and daily activities. People have been urged to monitor official forecasts, avoid unnecessary travel and stay away from flood-prone riverbanks.

Editorial Analysis Why This Matters Tourist safety: Snowstorms and avalanches can turn routine mountain journeys into life-threatening situations. Trekking operators: Agencies may need to revise itineraries, coordinate with guides and communicate changes to clients. Local communities: Weather-related transport disruptions can affect access to remote settlements and tourism-dependent businesses. Travel planning: Visitors need to check permit eligibility, route conditions and weather advisories before leaving. Emergency preparedness: Following official warnings can reduce avoidable exposure to hazardous conditions.

title: Users turn to Nepal Telecom as private ISPs raise internet prices - The Kathmandu Post
description: Users turn to Nepal Telecom as private ISPs raise internet prices  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Private internet service providers are facing a backlash after withdrawing cheaper plans below 50 Mbps and raising tariffs, prompting some customers to switch to Nepal Telecom’s more affordable fibre service.

The state-owned telecom company’s annual 30 Mbps package, priced at Rs4,999 including free installation, has attracted growing interest. But some customers making the switch have complained about delays in customer support and questioned the quality of the service and equipment.

Nepal Telecom says demand for new connections has risen as much as threefold, forcing it to introduce a dedicated hotline and an online portal to manage enquiries and installation requests.

Arjun Tamang, from Nuwakot, said he tried to arrange a connection during the Dashain festival but struggled to reach customer support. An automated response told him he was 161st in the queue and would have to wait 16 minutes before speaking to a representative.

Dissatisfaction with private providers has also spread across social media. Anup Thakuri, a WorldLink customer, complained on Facebook that his monthly bill for a 50 Mbps Special BTL package had risen from Rs1,017 in September to Rs1,350 in October.

“How has the price of WorldLink Wi-Fi gone up like this? I used to pay Rs1,017 every month, but now it has suddenly jumped to Rs1,350,” he wrote. “Is it just me, or has everyone’s bill gone up?”

Consumers have taken to Facebook and X to protest what they say are unannounced price increases and the withdrawal of cheaper packages. Students and people on lower incomes are among those affected by the removal of plans offering speeds below 50 Mbps.

Soon after private providers announced the changes, Nepal Telecom introduced its discounted festive-season offer, giving customers an alternative as frustration over private ISPs’ tariffs mounted.

The increased interest has translated into a sharp rise in demand for Nepal Telecom’s fibre connections. Prakshet Thapa Chhetri, the company’s assistant spokesperson, said requests for new connections had tripled compared with previous levels.

The number of new connections, which averaged 3,000 a month in the two preceding months, doubled to 6,000 in mid-September to mid-October, he said.

The company has received particularly strong demand from densely populated urban areas, including Kathmandu. Its Dashain-Tihar offer provides a 30 Mbps NT Fibre connection for Rs4,999 a year, with the installation fee waived.

Interest remained high throughout Dashain after Prime Minister Balendra Shah shared a poster promoting the offer on his Facebook page on October 9, the company said. “Having the prime minister, who has a large social media following and considerable popularity, promote the offer has been a big help with marketing,” Thapa said. “It has made more consumers aware of the affordable package and directly contributed to the rise in demand for NT Fibre.”

Soon after Shah shared the poster, however, the Nepal Telecommunications Authority fined Nepal Telecom and five other service providers Rs50,000 each for operating services in breach of licence conditions.

The regulatory action followed a report by TechPana that the package had been announced without the authority’s approval. Nepal Telecom subsequently issued a statement saying it had already informed the regulator about the offer.

Sanjay Mahato, from Tandi in Chitwan, also shared his experience of switching to Nepal Telecom, saying he had bought a one-year fibre package on October 17 after private providers raised their prices. But he cautioned other customers about the router supplied with the Rs4,999 package. In a social media post, he alleged that customers opting for the 30 Mbps plan were being given old, single-band routers returned by other users, while those subscribing to the 50 Mbps plan received new dual-band devices.

“It turns out they give customers old single-band routers returned by other users in the name of offering a cheaper package,” he wrote. “Customers taking the 50 Mbps plan get a new dual-band router, but those opting for 30 Mbps are given old single-band ones.”

Asked about complaints over service quality, Thapa said Nepal Telecom was not compromising on standards. The company already had sufficient network capacity to handle the surge in demand, he said, adding that the increase in new connections would not affect internet speeds or service quality.

The company has also reported a sharp rise in calls to its hotline, 198, for enquiries and new connection requests.

Meanwhile, some users have been using public Facebook groups to challenge the government over its perceived silence on rising internet tariffs. They argue that prices have increased even as the administration, which benefited from strong social media support, has promoted the state-owned provider’s offer.

Shankar Karki, an administrator of the Vianet Internet Users Group, has repeatedly criticised the price increases.

“Since the new government took office, internet prices have risen and competition has effectively stopped,” he wrote. “Until a few months ago, ISPs were offering various deals. Now, they have raised prices by 50, 55, 60 or even 100 percent. Does the Balendra government, which promotes Nepal Telecom’s advertisements, know nothing about this?”

title: Nepal's Climate Diplomacy - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal's Climate Diplomacy  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Climate change has lately emerged as a key agenda in the world. Until the late 20th century, this issue had been narrowly defined as a domain of science. Now environment and climate change no longer remain to be scientific connotation alone but topic of household talks. It has been a key part of political, economic, foreign policy, security, human rights, development, and diplomatic agendas.

The world seems to be nearing the climate tipping point, which has raised greater alarm worldwide. Scientists and environmentalists are of the view that Earth’s temperature has been at an alarming level that was not felt for millions of years. If the present trend of greenhouse gas emissions and temperature rise continues unabated, the human species may see its extinction soon. This is therefore humanity’s existential issue. However, some countries, especially in the Global North, appear to be hesitant to take this matter with utmost seriousness.

Massive deforestation

Climate change is caused by a global temperature rise. The average temperature is rising every year due mainly to the burning of carbon-based fuels, massive deforestation, and other human activities in the name of development. All human beings are, in one way or another, responsible for global warming in general, but the Global North and fossil fuel-producing countries are more accountable. The global temperature has risen at the rate of about 0.2 degrees Celsius per decade compared to the pre-industrial period (1850–1900). Earth is facing the climate change consequences in multiple forms, including cyclones, floods, landslides, snow melting, drying of water sources, drought, changes in weather patterns, and sea level rise, among many. The developing and the least developed countries are facing more recurrent climate change-induced challenges and threats due to the mistakes they did not commit. Instead, the countries in the Global South are suffering from the crimes committed by others.

As the threat of environmental degradation and climate change continues to afflict the world, there has been greater advocacy to address climate change issues globally. Right from the 19th century, scientists have been working in this field and have established the connection between carbon emissions and global temperature rise. Now countries have taken this issue in national and international forums with more seriousness. This is how environmental and climate change issues started emerging as a key agenda in international politics and diplomacy.

The real momentum picked up in the late 20th century. As governments emphasized development and industrialization, its resultant impacts, including a high degree of pollution, deforestation, and depletion of natural resources, were visibly felt worldwide, leading to changes in the global climate and weather patterns in a more recurrent manner. In 1972, the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment was held in Stockholm, Sweden. This event served as a milestone in establishing the environment as a key topic of international diplomacy. The World Meteorological Organization, a specialized agency of the United Nations, organized the first World Climate Conference in Geneva, Switzerland, in 1979 that laid the foundation for the Rio Earth Summit.

As environmental and climate change emerged as an important agenda in international politics and diplomacy, the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations Environment Programme created a new mechanism called the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in 1988, intending to conduct more scientific research on the impact of climate change on human life and development. IPCC prepared a report in 1990 recommending the urgency of collaboration from all countries on the climate change issue.

The UN Conference on Environment and Development, known as the Earth Summit, was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 1992, which is another important landmark in climate diplomacy. The Earth Summit created the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which entered into force in 1994. Ever since, UNFCCC holds annual Conference of the parties or COP to assess the developments in climate change regime and renew commitment to reduce greenhouse gas emission target.

The Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997, is yet another important step towards international climate diplomacy, which set legally binding greenhouse-gas emission-lowering targets. The Paris Agreement, adopted at COP21 in 2015, is yet another turning point in international climate diplomacy, which set binding targets of keeping global average temperature rise below 2°Celcius compared to the level of the pre-industrial era and pursue efforts to ultimately limit it to 1.5°C.

Since COP1 in Berlin, UN has been holding conference of parties or COP annually, which is good international forum for climate diplomacy. COP31 is being held in Antalya, Turkey, on 9-20 November 2026, which is expected to set future action plans on the international climate regime.

Nepal first joined the international environment and climate discourse in 1972 at the Stockholm Conference and the UNFCCC in 1992. Since then, Nepal has been actively participating in the UN and other international climate diplomacy discourse and has presented its voice on the impacts suffered due to climate change. But there has been stark weakness and glaring lacuna in follow-ups and inter-ministerial coordination on climate diplomacy. Foreign Ministry is the frontline institution of the country’s diplomacy, but the climate issue is considered to be the domain of other ministries.

Human survival

After the recent Bhotekoshi and Budhigandaki disasters, climate diplomacy has emerged as a popular term in Nepal’s intellectual discourse. Climate is no longer an environmental issue but a question of human survival. Climate change has been a matter of human security as it is going to affect the entire humanity. If not addressed in time, the world may face acute water and food scarcity, health hazards, housing problems, mass migration and displacement by floods and landslides, sea level rise, social conflict, and extreme weather conditions, among others. The climate change issue, therefore, must be addressed at the earliest by adopting measures to reduce greenhouse emission including reduction of burning excessive fossil fuel, exploring more green energy sources and remodelling development projects.

The new government headed by Prime Minister Balendra Shah seems to be giving higher priority to climate diplomacy. PM Shah put forth Nepal’s voice strongly in the UN General Assembly, which was quickly responded to by the international community with a decision to grant Nepal 20 million dollars from the UNFCCC Loss and Damage Fund. Although this is a drop in the bucket compared to the loss Nepal incurred, this is a good beginning. The government now needs to pursue further with utmost seriousness in all diplomatic negotiations that can help bridge the resource gap by facilitating more flow of climate funding.





(The author is a former chief editor of this daily and a former ambassador. lamsalyubanath@gmail.com)

title: Could Rahul Yadav be Nepali cricket’s next big thing? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Could Rahul Yadav be Nepali cricket’s next big thing?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
“He stood out through the fitness tests, the cricket trials, and showed the skill, hunger and determination we were looking for.” That was how Janakpur Bolts proudly announced 17-year-old Rahul Yadav as their “iconic player” for the third season on the evening of October 25.

Two days later, Yadav did more than make his Nepal Premier League debut. He took two wickets and conceded just two runs in the two overs he bowled during the powerplay.

There was a stir in the media box when journalists received the line-ups for Karnali Yaks and Janakpur Bolts on their phones and saw Yadav in the playing XI.

The Bolts won the toss and captain Harmeet Singh elected to bowl first.

Veteran England all-rounder Moeen Ali opened the bowling for Janakpur and dismissed the dangerous Mark Watt. Nepal’s experienced spinner Lalit Narayan Rajbanshi bowled the second over, in which Deepak Dumre struck two consecutive sixes.

Dumre took a single off the final delivery, keeping the strike for the third over. Then came the surprise: 17-year-old Yadav was handed the ball.

Less than a month earlier, Yadav had been playing on the uneven, open cricket grounds of Rautahat. Now he was bowling in front of thousands of fans at TU International Cricket Stadium in Kirtipur, a venue many aspiring Nepali cricketers dream of reaching.

It was a stage Yadav, too, had dreamed of playing on.

His Facebook profile picture shows him holding a man-of-the-match award from the Chandrapur Cricket League 2082. The caption reads, “Pp change after long time”, followed by emojis. After his performance against Karnali, he may have several new photographs to choose from.

Yadav looked composed as he took the ball and began his short run-up, seemingly unfazed by the presence of fast-bowling great Shoaib Akhtar.

A right-arm medium pacer, Yadav put his body into the delivery to generate pace. He bowled short, tempting Dumre to cut the ball. But a bottom edge sent it on to the stumps, giving Yadav a wicket with his very first delivery in the NPL.

His impressive debut did not end there.

Dumre was replaced by Hussain Talat, the experienced Pakistani all-rounder. Yadav kept the senior batter in check. After four consecutive dot balls, Talat finally got off the mark with a single off the last ball of the over.

Jimmy Neesham and Moeen Ali bowled the fourth and fifth overs, respectively, conceding a six each. Karnali were then 37 for 2, with Ariful Islam on 19 off nine balls and Talat on three off 11.

Singh turned to the teenager again for the final over of the powerplay, and Yadav delivered once more. After two dot balls, Talat, under pressure to score, was caught by Anil Kumar Sah. Yadav conceded just one run in the over.

His four overs cost only 15 runs and brought two wickets, playing a key role in restricting Karnali to 132 for 9.

Janakpur could not chase the target. They were bowled out for 113 in 19.3 overs, losing by 19 runs. Yadav was the only Janakpur batter left unbeaten, finishing on one off 10 balls.

He came in at No. 10 with Karnali bowler Unish Bikram Singh Thakuri on a hat-trick after dismissing Jimmy Neesham and Aaditya Mahata with the first two balls of the 16th over. With his team in trouble, Yadav survived the next three deliveries before taking a single off the final ball to give Abhishekh Tiwari the strike. Tiwari went on to hit two sixes.

Janakpur lost, but Yadav had given the franchise plenty of reason to be encouraged by his performance.

“I will give my 100 percent for the team,” Yadav said in a video posted by Janakpur Bolts, responding to a question about what he would do if selected.

In the video, published on October 16, Yadav was among seven teenagers selected from across Madhesh Province through the franchise’s Talent Hunt. They were placed in the Bolts’ “development squad”, a group of promising players set to train alongside the main squad throughout the tournament.

The other six players in the development squad are Aadarsha Bhandari, Khil Raj Sharraf, Navin Kumar Yadav, Rohan Kumar Sah, Md Miraj and Sushant Singh.

Janakpur’s decision to name Yadav its “iconic player” and include him in the starting XI quickly looked justified. The franchise’s captain was impressed, too.

“I think he is very deceptive, and someone who has never played him would always find it difficult in the first few balls,” Singh said at the post-match press conference.

title: China steps up engagement with Nepal’s ruling party - The Annapurna Express
description: China steps up engagement with Nepal’s ruling party  The Annapurna Express
publisher.title: The Annapurna Express
full_article:
A delegation from Nepal’s ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), led by General Secretary Bipin Kumar Acharya, is scheduled to visit China in the second week of November at the invitation of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC).

During the visit, the delegation is expected to travel to several Chinese cities to observe the country’s development and infrastructure, according to information about the planned trip.

Since the RSP came to power, the CPC has stepped up its engagement with the party’s leaders. Visits by RSP leaders to China have also increased in recent months, signalling Beijing’s growing efforts to strengthen ties with Nepal’s ruling party.

Earlier this month, RSP Deputy Leader Ganesh Parajuli led a delegation to China to participate in a programme organised by the Chinese government.

There had also been discussions about a possible visit to China by RSP President Rabi Lamichhane. However, the visit has been delayed, and the party has not publicly explained the reason for the postponement.

China has traditionally maintained close relations with Nepal’s communist parties and the Nepali Congress. However, Beijing appears to be broadening its political engagement by reaching out to the RSP while continuing its interactions with established political parties.

In a recent development, senior CPN-UML leader Bidya Devi Bhandari visited China, highlighting Beijing’s continued engagement with leaders across Nepal’s political spectrum.

The planned visit by the RSP delegation comes amid growing diplomatic and political engagement between China and Nepal’s ruling party. The visit is expected to provide the delegation with an opportunity to observe China’s development model and further strengthen ties between the RSP and the CPC.

The visit comes at a time of growing political mistrust between the leadership of the two countries, amid a slowdown in bilateral engagement.

title: Nepal urges trekkers to suspend activities amid cyclone threat - chinadailyhk
description: Nepal urges trekkers to suspend activities amid cyclone threat  chinadailyhk

full_article:
A tourist enjoys the view of mountain ranges seen from Ama Yangri Peak, about 84 kilometers north of Kathmandu, Nepal, April 4, 2026. (PHOTO/AP)

KATHMANDU – Nepal's Department of Immigration on Tuesday urged trekkers to suspend trekking activities in high-altitude mountainous and Himalayan regions amid forecasts of heavy rainfall and snowfall as Cyclone Arnab intensifies over the Bay of Bengal.

Several provinces of the country were likely to experience heavy rainfall, while higher hilly areas and the Himalayan regions were expected to receive snowfall, the department said in a statement.

In view of the forecast for three days starting Thursday, trekkers who have obtained permits to visit high-altitude mountainous and Himalayan regions are requested to refrain from trekking to minimize potential risks, the statement said.

READ MORE: More than 100 foreign trekkers stranded in flood-hit region of Nepal, official says

Trekkers who have already embarked on their journeys have been urged to remain in safe locations throughout the period.

The department also announced that trekking permits for restricted areas in high-altitude mountainous and Himalayan regions would not be issued during the period, with the measure taking effect on Tuesday. It has urged the trekking agencies, trekkers, guides and other concerned stakeholders to comply with the notice.

According to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the cyclone is forecast to make landfall in India on Wednesday, with its impact expected to be felt in Nepal from Thursday night.
